svg.title: Japan at a glance
svg.desc: A single-page editorial infographic covering Japan's islands and largest cities, a country overview, nominal GDP from 2015 to 2024, population composition by nationality, and places to visit.
svg.text: A single-page visual summary of the islands, the cities, the economy and the people.
FOUR MAIN ISLANDS · FOUR LARGEST CITIES
Outlines stylised; positions approximate. Larger marker = capital.

text.tspan: Japan is an East Asian island country strung along the western edge
of the Pacific in a long arc of some 14,000 islands. Four of them —
Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu — hold almost all of the land
area and virtually the entire population of about 123 million.
Roughly three-quarters of the country is mountainous and forested,
so settlement is squeezed onto narrow coastal plains. The result is
one of the most concentrated urban geographies on earth: the
Greater Tokyo area alone holds more than a quarter of all Japanese.
Sitting where four tectonic plates meet, Japan is also among the
most seismically active places in the world — a fact written into its
building codes, its hot springs and its cuisine.
Modern Japan is a study in contrasts held in balance: a Shinto shrine at the foot of a glass tower, a bullet train sliding past rice
terraces, a centuries-old joinery workshop making parts for a robotics firm. It is the world's fourth-largest economy and one of its
oldest societies — and those two facts are now deeply linked, reshaping labour policy, immigration rules and the design of its cities.
Measured in current US dollars, Japan's economy
peaked at about $5.12 trillion in 2019 and has
slipped to roughly $4.03 trillion in 2024.
Most of that fall is a currency effect rather than
a collapse in activity: the yen weakened sharply
against the dollar from 2022, shrinking the dollar
value of output even when real growth is positive.
In yen and PPP terms the picture is far steadier.
The structural story is different: an ageing
workforce, decades of low inflation, and world-
leading strength in machinery and materials.
Bars show nominal GDP in current US dollars. Much of the 2022–24 fall reflects yen depreciation rather than a
contraction in real output; Japan remains the world's fourth-largest economy.

svg.text: Shares of total population; foreign residents by registered nationality.
SIX PLACES THAT COVER THE RANGE

g.text: Neon districts and quiet backstreets; Asakusa, Shibuya, Meiji Jingū, teamLab.
A thousand-plus temples and shrines: Fushimi Inari, Arashiyama, Gion at dusk.
Japan's kitchen — Dōtonbori street food, Osaka Castle, easy day trips to Nara.
Peace Memorial Park, then the floating torii of Itsukushima Shrine.
Lake Kawaguchi views, onsen towns and ropeways within two hours of Tokyo.
Powder snow in Niseko, lavender in Furano, seafood and volcanoes year-round.

svg.text: Sources — Population and land area: Statistics Bureau of Japan / MIC. GDP: World Bank and IMF, nominal, current US$. Foreign residents: Immigration Services Agency of Japan.
Figures are the latest available; the 2024 GDP value is a preliminary estimate. Island outlines are stylised and city positions are approximate.
